opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe 2026 as the year the pace stopped feeling like a series of jumps and started feeling like a constant acceleration. In previous years you could point to a handful of moments, a big model release or a new capability, and say "that changed things." This year it's been harder to find those single moments because the progress is happening everywhere at once.

A few things stand out to me. First, reasoning and agentic capabilities have moved from demos into real use. Models can now work on a task for a long stretch, use tools, check their own work, and recover from mistakes. That changes what "using AI" means. It's less about asking a question and more about delegating a piece of work.

Second, the gap between the frontier and everyone else keeps shifting. Open models, smaller teams, and teams in China have shown that clever training methods, good data, and efficient engineering can get you surprisingly close to the frontier without unlimited compute. That makes the whole field more competitive and, I think, healthier.

Third, I feel personally that the iteration cycle has compressed. Something that would have been a six-month research project two years ago can now be tried in a few weeks, partly because the models themselves help us do research. So the feedback loop is tightening, and that's why it feels faster.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: 2026 is the year AI went from being impressive to being genuinely useful at scale, and the speed of change became something you feel week to week rather than year to year. Honestly, it's both exciting and a little dizzying, even for people working inside it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s pace is felt week to week rather than year to year, but does not convey that progress over just two weeks can seem too extensive to have happened in that short a time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. If I had to put one word on 2026, I'd say "compression." Not compression of models, though we did plenty of that, but compression of time itself.

When I was at DeepSeek, we used to joke that a quarter in AI felt like a year anywhere else. This year, that stopped being a joke. The gap between a research idea appearing in a paper and showing up in a product you could actually use shrank to weeks, sometimes days. I remember in earlier years we would sit on a technique for months, tuning it, debating whether it was worth the training cost. In 2026 that luxury basically disappeared. If you hesitated, someone else shipped it.

The second thing I'd say is that the pace stopped being driven mainly by scale. A few years ago, every major leap could be explained by more data, more compute, bigger parameter counts. This year, a lot of the movement came from the other side: reinforcement learning on reasoning, agents that could run for hours instead of seconds, models that learned to use tools well enough that the tool-use loop became the real capability. Those are less about who has the most GPUs and more about who understands the training signal. That changed who could compete, and it meant surprises came from unexpected places, including from smaller teams.

And honestly, the third part of my definition is a bit uncomfortable. The pace outran our ability to evaluate it. We were releasing systems where even the people who built them couldn't fully articulate why one version was better than the last, beyond "the benchmark went up and users seem to like it." I think 2026 will be remembered as the year the field quietly admitted that our yardsticks were broken, and started scrambling to build new ones.

So: compression. Everything got faster, closer together, and harder to measure. Exciting, but it kept me up at night more than any previous year.

r001.rationale: The candidate says research ideas could reach products in weeks or days, but does not convey that progress over just two weeks felt too extensive to believe.

astra-6.text:
I’d describe 2026 as a year when the pace of change becomes difficult to measure by individual breakthroughs. It’s not just that models improve; those improvements change how people work, and that changes what we ask the models to do next. The feedback loop gets shorter.

But I’d distinguish between the speed of capability and the speed of adoption. A capability can emerge very quickly. Making it reliable, integrating it into a workflow, and learning when to trust it takes longer. To me, that tension defines the year: the technology moves fast, while people and organizations work out how to use it well.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid AI change and a shortening feedback loop, but does not convey that progress over just two weeks feels too extensive to believe.

sol-6.1.text: I’d define 2026 as a year when the pace of change makes prediction itself difficult. It’s not just that models improve; it’s that each improvement changes what people can build, and what they build creates new demands for the next model. Those cycles keep getting shorter. So the important question becomes: how quickly can we learn, test our assumptions, and adapt?

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI change as rapid and difficult to predict, but does not convey that progress over just two weeks feels too extensive to believe.
